title: UAV² Unified Adaptive Scheduling for Drone Flight
one_liner: Teach a drone's onboard computer what order to run its navigation and steering tasks by watching how well the drone flies, instead of using fixed timing rules.
lead: Drones need two things happening constantly: figuring out where to go next (navigation) and actually steering the aircraft (flight control). Right now, most drones run these on separate chips, so no one piece of code can coordinate them together. This paper moves them onto one computer and uses a learning system (a program that adjusts its decisions based on feedback) that watches the drone's flight path accuracy to discover which order of tasks keeps the drone on course best.

paras: Every drone has two jobs running all the time. Navigation asks: Where am I? Where do I want to go? What is the next target? Flight control asks: How do I angle the motors right now to actually get there? Most drone platforms split these between two separate computers, like having a car's GPS on one device and the steering wheel on another.

When the two are separate, nothing sees the whole picture. If the navigation gets delayed by one millisecond and the steering doesn't know, the drone wobbles. If the flight control is tuned too aggressively and navigation is too slow to keep up, they fight each other and the drone crashes or drifts. A beginner might say: just run both as fast as possible, or run them on a fixed schedule like every 10 milliseconds. But these do not work because sometimes navigation needs more time to think (the world is complex), sometimes flight control needs to run more often (turbulence is here now), and the two interact in hidden ways.

callout.html: The paper puts navigation and flight control on one computer and learns the best switching schedule by watching how well the drone actually flies.

steps.text: Navigation and flight control run on the same onboard computer, so decisions are synchronized.
At each moment, pick which task runs next (navigation or flight control) to minimize how far the drone drifts from its target.
As the drone completes each short cycle, measure how well it tracked its path.
When a task order leads to lower drift, increase the weight on that choice, because lower drift means the drone is following commands more accurately.
Over many flights, which tasks to run first in different situations becomes clear because the weighting pushes toward orders that reduce drift.

paras: The paper changes the scheduling decision — which task runs at which moment in the onboard computer's cycle. Instead of a fixed sequence (like navigation, then flight control, then navigation again every fixed 10 milliseconds), the scheduler learns to pick each task adaptively based on how well the drone is currently flying.

hidden.h2: Flight tracking error — the signal the system learns from
hidden.name: tracking error per cycle
paras: The hidden quantity is how far the drone actually strayed from its intended path in this one cycle, measured in meters or attitude angle. This is not the same as the problem statement — we are not looking at why scheduling fails in general, we are looking at the specific number the learning system uses to decide if a schedule choice was good.

The paper estimates this by running the drone in simulation (a hardware-in-the-loop test bench where the autopilot software runs on real chips but the physics is simulated) and recording position and heading after each cycle. The learning system uses this error signal to rank different scheduling choices: if task order A produces smaller tracking error than task order B, the system will gradually favor A in future flights because a smaller error means the drone is obeying commands more precisely.

heat.caption: Darker cells have more impact on which schedule the system learns.

reads.html: A drone trying to hold steady above one spot will drift left, right, up, or down. After each decision cycle, measure that drift in centimeters. That drift is the tracking error. The smaller the drift, the better the schedule choice was, because a schedule that causes the drone to drift less is letting it follow its target more accurately.

The learning system formulates the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process (a standard way to model decisions where you do not see the full state but can measure outcomes). The reward signal is negative tracking error — the learning system wants to minimize how far the drone strays.

mechanism.h2: How changing the schedule fixes the problem
paras: The core mechanism is tight feedback: each time the drone completes a cycle, the system immediately knows whether that schedule choice was good (small error) or bad (large error). Because the two tasks are now on one computer, the scheduler can react instantly if it realizes navigation is falling behind or flight control is stale. In contrast, the old separate-computer design had no way to know; each computer just did its thing on its fixed schedule.

The learning system (called reinforcement learning) works like this: try a scheduling order, watch the drone's error shrink or grow, and then nudge the system's decision weights toward choices that led to smaller errors. Over hundreds of flights in simulation, this nudging finds schedules that balance the two competing demands — sometimes navigation needs the computer first to think ahead, sometimes flight control needs it to respond to immediate wobble. A fixed schedule can never adapt to these changing demands; a learning system can.

stages.s: Drone state: position, heading, sensor readings
Scheduler picks next task (navigation or flight control)
Task runs on one shared computer
Next cycle uses adjusted task order because low error steered weights toward this choice

math.words: Total reward equals the negative of tracking error, minus a small cost for computational work.
symbols: how far drone drifted from target
computational load of running both tasks
how much to penalize high CPU usage (tuning knob)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Cycle A: navigation runs, then flight control. Drift = 2 centimeters. Work = 80% CPU. Reward = -2 - 0.1 * 80 = -10.0
Cycle B: flight control runs, then navigation. Drift = 0.5 centimeters. Work = 75% CPU. Reward = -0.5 - 0.1 * 75 = -8.0
Cycle B has higher (less negative) reward, so learning nudges the system toward that order.

math.note: The learning system collects these rewards over many cycles and adjusts its scheduling choices to maximize cumulative reward — that is, to keep drift small and CPU usage reasonable.

charts.title: Fixed every-10ms schedule
charts.note: Fixed timing cannot adapt when the drone's needs change.

charts.title: Learned adaptive schedule
charts.note: Learned scheduling reduces drift in all flight regimes.

items.b: Learning only in simulation, not on a real drone.
items.html: The system is trained in a simulated physics world (hardware-in-the-loop), so it may overfit to quirks of that simulation. Wind, real-world sensor noise, or motor delays might differ, causing the learned schedule to fail on actual hardware.

items.b: Hidden interdependencies between navigation and flight control.
items.html: The paper treats them as two separate tasks, but in reality they might have complex feedback loops (flight wobbles affect sensor readings, which affect navigation). The learning system might not discover these interactions if they are rare or delayed.

items.b: Tuning the learning rate and reward weights is manual.
items.html: The coefficients in the reward formula (how much to penalize CPU work, for example) are set by hand. A wrong setting can trap the learning system in a local optimum or cause instability.

Train on a diverse set of simulated scenarios (calm air, wind, heavy load, lightweight), test on trajectories the learning system never saw, and gradually increase the gap between simulation and reality to catch brittleness early.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple drone autopilot simulator (a 2D position-and-heading model that responds to navigation and flight-control inputs). Create two drones: one with a fixed schedule (navigation, then flight control, alternating every 50 milliseconds) and one with a learned schedule trained on 100 simulated flights. Fly both drones along the same path (e.g., follow a square, hover in wind, track a moving target). Measure position drift over 60 seconds for each.
demo.metric_eq: Mean tracking error = sum of (distance from target after each cycle) divided by number of cycles
demo.closing: The learned schedule must show smaller mean drift than the fixed schedule. Ideally, show a plot of drift over time: the fixed schedule should oscillate and grow, while the learned schedule should stay low and stable.
